In this section we are going to look at grid algorithm.
What is grid algorithm.
Now to understand this let's look at the real life example.
So we are going to use the building a wall with broken bricks.
This analogy helps us to simplify how grid algorithm works and why it can be effective.
So let's look at this scenario.
So let's say you have a pile of broken bricks, each with different shapes and levels of damage, and
your task is to build a solid wall out of them.
Now for a moment, let's forget about the grid algorithm.
Let's think about a common sense.
So when you build a wall from the broken bricks, you start building by choosing the best available
brick in each step, one that's the most solid or least broken at that moment.
You don't have time to evaluate every single brick in the pile.
You just need to choose the best one you find for each step as you go along.
So the steps is going to be like this.
First, we are going to look at the pile and choose the best available brick to place as the first brick
in the wall.
Then after placing the first brick, we are going to find the next best one in the pile and add it to
the wall.
And we are going to repeat this process each time, choosing the best remaining brick you can find to
continue building the wall.
In each step, you are selecting locally optimal choice, which is the best brick you can see.
At that moment.
You are not trying to analyze all bricks in advance or plan where every brick should go.
Instead, you are building the wall one step at a time.
Now the question is how this relates to the grid algorithm.
A grid algorithm builds a solution piece by piece, by always choosing the option that looks the best
in the specific step.
So, as it says in the definition of the grid algorithm, it constructs the solution step by step,
always choosing the most immediate advantage or the best local solution available at each step.
So in our example, we were choosing the best brick you can find at each stage.
Then each choice of brick is the best one for the immediate task.
So this means that grid algorithm focuses on the short term benefits to build the complete solution.
Then at the end, each layer in the wall represents a local solution and built by choosing the best
bricks for that row.
And in the third step, we are combining the local to reach the global.
So in our case, each layer in the wall represents a local solution by building the best bricks for
the row.
Then when all layers are completed, you get a full wall, which is a global solution.
The greedy approach works here because the local optimal choices combined to create the desired global
output.
Not all problems can be solved this way, but the greedy approach works in cases where these local choices
lead to the global optimum solution.
